name: Hellifield engine shed
text: Your train passes the site of the old engine shed, on the train's {side}, opened in 1880 and closed in 1963. Its most important job was to provide extra engines to help trains up the Long Drag, the climb that runs all the way to Ais Gill on the line to Carlisle.

name: Bell Busk
text: Your train passes near Bell Busk, on the train's {side}, a hamlet where the young River Aire meets Otterburn Beck. Its name is thought to come from Old Norse and Old English for a bell-shaped bush; in 1781 a weir and mill pond were built on the Aire to power a silk mill.

name: Roman villa at Kirk Sink
text: Your train passes near the site of a Roman villa at Kirk Sink, on the train's {side}, built in the second century in flat meadows by the River Aire. Dug up between 1968 and 1974, it had a central room with a mosaic floor seven metres square, and a bath house alongside.

name: Skipton General Hospital
text: Your train passes Skipton General Hospital, on the train's {side}, in Whinfield House, once the home of the mill owner Thomas Dewhurst. The house was opened as a hospital by the Princess Royal in 1932, replacing a cottage hospital opened in 1899 by the pioneer of women's education Lucy Cavendish.

name: Kildwick Bridge
text: Your train passes near Kildwick Bridge, on the train's {side}, built in stone over the River Aire between 1305 and 1313 at the expense of Bolton Priory. The oldest bridge in Airedale, it is really two bridges side by side: the upstream side with its pointed arches is the original, and the other was added when the road was widened in 1780.

name: Cliffe Castle Museum
text: Your train passes near Cliffe Castle, on the train's {side}, built as Cliffe Hall between 1828 and 1833. The textile manufacturer Henry Isaac Butterfield added towers, a ballroom and conservatories and renamed it a castle in 1878; since 1959 it has been Keighley's museum.

name: Dalton Mills
text: Your train passes near Dalton Mills, on the train's {side}, a worsted mill built in 1869 by Joseph Craven and once said to be the largest textile mill in Yorkshire, with more than 2,000 workers. Listed Grade II*, it has been used as a set for Peaky Blinders.

name: Bingley Five Rise Locks
text: Your train passes near the Five Rise Locks, on the train's {side}, a staircase of five locks on the Leeds and Liverpool Canal and the steepest flight of locks in the UK. When they opened on March 21st 1774, a crowd of 30,000 turned out, and the first boat took just 28 minutes to pass through.

name: Saltaire United Reformed Church
text: Your train passes the United Reformed Church, on the train's {side}, the first public building Titus Salt commissioned for his model village of Saltaire. He gave the land and paid the whole £16,000 himself; it is listed Grade I.

name: Salts Mill
text: Your train passes Salts Mill, on the train's {side}, opened by Sir Titus Salt in 1853, when it was the largest industrial building in the world by floor area. It closed in 1986 and is now an art gallery, shops and a restaurant, with many paintings by David Hockney on show.

name: Shipley Clock Tower
text: Your train passes near Shipley Clock Tower, on the train's {side}, built in 1960 and 1961 in the Festival of Britain style as the centrepiece of a new shopping centre, which the television presenter Bruce Forsyth opened in 1961.

name: Bradford Beck
text: Your train passes near Bradford Beck, on the train's {side}, on its way to join the River Aire. Bradford is named after a broad ford across it, and it was once known as the filthiest river in England; in the city centre it still runs underground.

name: Thackley Tunnel
text: Your train runs through Thackley Tunnel under Thackley Hill, opened in 1846 on Robert Stephenson's route along the Aire Valley. A second tunnel was dug beside it in 1900, when the line was widened to four tracks; that one closed in 1968.

name: Woodhouse Grove School
text: Your train passes near Woodhouse Grove School, on the train's {side}, opened on January 8th 1812 for the sons of Methodist ministers, with 27 pupils sleeping in wooden cots and a barn cleaned up as their schoolroom. It now teaches about 1,000 girls and boys.

name: St Oswald's Church, Guiseley
text: Your train passes near St Oswald's Church, on the train's {side}, which dates back to the late 11th or early 12th century and is listed Grade I. Patrick Brontë married Maria Branwell here on December 29th 1812.

name: Esholt
text: Your train passes near Esholt, on the train's {side}, a village named after the ash trees it was built among. From 1976 to 1996 it was the outdoor setting for the television series Emmerdale Farm, and it appeared again in an episode of 2016.

name: High Royds Hospital Railway
text: Your train passes near the route of the High Royds Hospital Railway, on the train's {side}, a short single-track branch opened in 1883 to carry building materials, then coal and flour, up to the county asylum. It was electrified in 1897 and closed for good in 1951.

name: Scalebor Park Hospital
text: Your train passes near the site of Scalebor Park Hospital, on the train's {side}, opened in 1902 as the West Riding Private Asylum for paying patients. It closed in 1995, and its main block was turned into flats in 2001.

name: Ben Rhydding Hydro
text: Your train passes near the site of the Ben Rhydding Hydro, on the train's {side}, opened on March 29th 1844 for the Victorian cold water cure. It was the first purpose-built hydropathic hotel in the UK, and gave its name to the village, then called Wheatley; it was pulled down in 1955.

name: Manor House, Ilkley
text: Your train passes near the Manor House, on the train's {side}, one of Ilkley's oldest buildings, listed Grade I and now a museum and art gallery. It stands on the site of a Roman fort, whose remains can be seen behind it.

name: Kirkstall Abbey
text: Your train passes near Kirkstall Abbey, on the train's {side}, the ruins of a Cistercian monastery whose monks came here from Barnoldswick in 1152. Closed under Henry VIII, the ruins were painted by J. M. W. Turner, Thomas Girtin and John Sell Cotman.

name: Tower Works
text: Your train passes near Tower Works, on the train's {side}, a factory that made steel pins for carding and combing in the textile trade. Its three towers took away the dust: the largest is modelled on Giotto's bell tower in Florence, and the boiler house chimney on the Torre dei Lamberti in Verona.

name: Stanningley
text: Your train passes near Stanningley, on the train's {side}, a district of Pudsey on the old main road from Leeds to Bradford. Its former St Paul's Church, built in 1853 and closed in 1982, was later used as offices by companies including the video game makers Rockstar Leeds.

name: Wool Exchange, Bradford
text: Your train passes near the Wool Exchange, on the train's {side}, built between 1864 and 1867 for the wool trade, its foundation stone laid by the Prime Minister, Lord Palmerston. John Ruskin, asked for advice, told Bradford: "I do not care about this Exchange – because you don't." It is now a bookshop.

name: National Science and Media Museum
text: Your train passes near the National Science and Media Museum, on the train's {side}, with seven floors of galleries on photography, film, television and video games. Its IMAX cinema, finished in April 1983, was the first in Europe.

name: Shibden Hall
text: Your train passes near Shibden Hall, on the train's {side}, a house dating back to about 1420 and known for its Tudor timbered front. Its most famous resident was the diarist Anne Lister, whose life was told in the television series Gentleman Jack, filmed here.

name: Piece Hall
text: Your train passes near the Piece Hall, on the train's {side}, built for handloom weavers to sell their pieces of woollen cloth. It opened on January 1st 1779 with 315 rooms round an open courtyard, and nobody knows for certain who designed it.

name: Halifax Minster
text: Your train passes near Halifax Minster, on the train's {side}, built in the 15th century where a church run by the monks of Lewes Priory stood from about 1120; carved stones from it survive in the walls. Inside are Jacobean box pews and the tombstone of the diarist Anne Lister.

name: Wood Lane Hall
text: Your train passes near Wood Lane Hall, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in stone in the 1650s for the clothier John Dearden; the date 1649 and the letters JDED, for John and Elizabeth Dearden, are over the door. With its rose window and battlements, it is listed Grade I.

name: Hebden Bridge signal box
text: Your train passes the old signal box at Hebden Bridge station, built in 1891 by the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway and one of few of its kind still much as it was. It was listed in 2013 and stopped working in October 2018, when signalling passed to York.

name: Todmorden Town Hall
text: Your train passes near the Town Hall, on the train's {side}, opened on April 3rd 1875 and listed Grade I. It was built across the Walsden Water, the old boundary between Yorkshire and Lancashire, and the Fielden family, who owned many of the town's cotton mills, paid for it.

name: Dobroyd Castle
text: Your train passes near Dobroyd Castle, on the train's {side}, built between 1866 and 1869 for the mill owner John Fielden. It is often said that Ruth Stansfield, a local worker, agreed to marry him only if he built her a castle; it has 66 rooms.

name: Tuel Lane Lock
text: Your train passes near Tuel Lane Lock, on the train's {side}, built in 1996 when the Rochdale Canal was restored. Replacing two of the old locks, it has a fall of about six metres, making it the deepest lock in the UK.

name: Rastrick Bridge
text: Your train passes near Rastrick Bridge, on the train's {side}, over the River Calder. A wooden bridge stood here by 1275; the first stone one was paid for in 1558 by the son of John Hanson, and it was rebuilt in about 1750.

name: Robin Hood's Grave
text: Your train passes near Robin Hood's Grave, on the train's {side}, in the Kirklees estate near the ruins of Kirklees Priory. Ballads tell how Robin, ill, was bled to death by the prioress, and in one version shot an arrow from his window to show where he should be buried; the stone was once chipped away as a cure for toothache.

name: Huddersfield station
text: Huddersfield station, at one end of this stretch, was designed by James Pigott Pritchett and built between 1846 and 1850. John Betjeman called its front the most splendid in England, and it is listed Grade I.

name: Milnsbridge
text: Your train passes Milnsbridge, on the train's {side}, crossing it on a viaduct. On June 24th 1931 the mill of Joseph Crowther and Sons here made a suit from sheep to wearer in two hours and ten minutes, beating the world record of six hours and four minutes.

name: George Hotel, Huddersfield
text: Your train passes near the George Hotel, on the train's {side}, built between 1848 and 1850 with an Italianate front. Rugby league began here at a meeting in 1895, and the hotel is full of reminders of it.

name: Slaithwaite
text: Your train passes near Slaithwaite, on the train's {side}, often pronounced "sla-wit". Legend has it that smugglers caught by the excise men claimed to be raking the moon out of the canal, not fishing out brandy, and every other February the town holds a Moonraking Festival with a lantern parade.

name: Lockwood Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Lockwood Viaduct over the River Holme, finished in 1848 and on average 37 metres high. A journalist once called it one of the most stupendous structures of ancient or modern times, and locals have long tried to lob a cricket ball over it.
